knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse   = TRUE,

  fig.width  = 8.888889,
  fig.height = 6.25,
  dpi        = 300

Four IPEDS surveys each capture a distinct dimension of rural higher education:
**where** institutions are, **what kind** they are, **how many degrees** they
confer, and **whether their students finish**. This vignette compares rural and
nonrural counties on each, then links degrees to the occupations they prepare
students for.

For an overview of the package (the surveys it covers, its county and institution levels, and its counting conventions), see
`vignette("introduction", package = "cori.data.ipeds")`.

```{r libraries}
library(cori.data.ipeds)
library(cori.data.pep)
library(ruraldefinitions)
library(cori.charts)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(scales)
library(stringr)

load_fonts()
```

```{r data}
YR <- 2024

degrees    <- get_degrees(years = YR)
completers <- get_completers(years = YR)
grad_rates <- get_graduation_rates(years = 2010:2023)

rural <- cbsa_2023 |>
  select(geoid, is_rural)
```

## Where the four-year institutions are

Identifying counties with a **four-year** institution requires institution-level
data, because the county-level variables count institutions without
distinguishing which ones offer bachelor's degrees.

```{r access}
has_university <- get_institutions(geography = "institution", years = YR) |>
  filter(is_degree_granting == 1, is_4yr == 1, !is.na(geoid)) |>
  distinct(geoid) |>
  mutate(has_university = TRUE)

access <- rural |>
  left_join(has_university, by = "geoid") |>
  mutate(has_university = coalesce(has_university, FALSE))

access |>
  group_by(is_rural) |>
  summarize(
    counties    = n(),
    with_uni    = sum(has_university),
    without     = sum(!has_university),
    pct_without = 100 * mean(!has_university),
    .groups     = "drop"
  )
#>   is_rural counties with_uni without pct_without
#>   Nonrural     1252      632     620         49.5
#>   Rural        1983      341    1642         82.8
```

Of the 973 counties nationally with a four-year institution, 341 (35%) are
rural. Another 227 rural counties have a degree-granting institution that offers
no bachelor's degree, bringing the number of rural counties with some
postsecondary capacity to 568.

```{r access-chart, echo = FALSE, eval = TRUE, out.width = "100%", fig.alt = "County choropleth map of the United States. Counties containing a four-year degree-granting university are colored, rural ones in green and nonrural in purple, against grey for counties without. Rural counties with a university appear as scattered isolated dots across largely empty interior regions."}
knitr::include_graphics("figures/access_map.png")
```

## What kind of institutions

The institution directory includes the flags used to build the county counts,
so level and control can be cross-tabulated.

```{r institution-type}
ic <- get_institutions(geography = "institution", years = YR) |>
  inner_join(rural, by = "geoid") |>
  # the level filter matters: without it, the 71 degree-granting
  # less-than-two-year institutions fall into the "Two-year" bucket
  filter(is_degree_granting == 1, is_4yr == 1 | is_2yr == 1) |>
  mutate(
    level   = if_else(is_4yr == 1, "Four-year", "Two-year"),
    control = if_else(is_public == 1, "Public", "Private")
  )

ic |>
  count(is_rural, level, control) |>
  group_by(is_rural) |>
  mutate(share = 100 * n / sum(n)) |>
  ungroup()
#>   is_rural level     control     n share
#>   Nonrural Four-year Private  1731  52.5
#>   Nonrural Four-year Public    647  19.6
#>   Nonrural Two-year  Private   442  13.4
#>   Nonrural Two-year  Public    480  14.5
#>   Rural    Four-year Private   212  29.6
#>   Rural    Four-year Public    199  27.8
#>   Rural    Two-year  Private    19   2.7
#>   Rural    Two-year  Public    286  39.9
```

The largest single category of nonrural institution is the private four-year
college, at 52.5%; the largest rural category is the public two-year college,
at 39.9%. Rural institutions are 67.7% public, compared with 34.2% of nonrural
institutions.

```{r institution-type-chart, echo = FALSE, eval = TRUE, out.width = "100%", fig.alt = "Faceted bar chart of institution shares by level and control. Among rural institutions the largest group is public two-year at 40 percent; among nonrural it is private four-year at 53 percent."}
knitr::include_graphics("figures/institution_type.png")
```

## Degrees conferred, per resident

Because `count_degrees_total` is a raw count, comparing counties requires a
denominator. Population comes from `cori.data.pep`, joined on `geoid`.

```{r per-capita}
pop <- get_population(geography = "county", years = YR) |>
  filter(variable == "population") |>
  select(geoid, population = value)

per_capita <- rural |>
  inner_join(pop, by = "geoid") |>
  left_join(
    degrees |> filter(variable == "count_degrees_total") |>
      select(geoid, degrees = value),
    by = "geoid"
  ) |>
  mutate(degrees = coalesce(degrees, 0))

per_capita |>
  group_by(is_rural) |>
  summarize(per_1k = 1000 * sum(degrees) / sum(population), .groups = "drop")
#>   is_rural per_1k
#>   Nonrural   12.5
#>   Rural       9.4
```

The aggregate rate hides wide variation. Plotted one dot per county, rates span
more than two orders of magnitude, with a long rural right tail: Merrimack
County, NH, confers 255 degrees per 1,000 residents; Whitley County, KY, 171;
and Whitman County, WA, 151.

```{r per-capita-chart, echo = FALSE, eval = TRUE, out.width = "100%", fig.alt = "Beeswarm plot of degrees conferred per 1,000 residents, one dot per county, on a log scale. Both rural and nonrural distributions are wide, with a long rural right tail."}
knitr::include_graphics("figures/per_capita.png")
```

This variable measures production, not attainment: degrees are credited to the
county where the institution is located, not where the student lives. Some
outliers reflect large online programs; Merrimack County's total, for example,
is driven largely by Southern New Hampshire University.

## How many students finish

`grad_rate_150pct` covers the full-time, first-time bachelor's cohort at
four-year institutions, and is already cohort-weighted within each county, so
aggregating across counties requires weighting by `agg_var`.

```{r grad-rates}
trend <- grad_rates |>
  filter(variable == "grad_rate_150pct") |>
  inner_join(rural, by = "geoid") |>
  group_by(year, is_rural) |>
  summarize(rate = sum(value * agg_var) / sum(agg_var), .groups = "drop")

# The same data, weighted and not, for 2023:
#   is_rural  weighted  unweighted
#   Nonrural      61.7        54.5
#   Rural         52.9        47.3
```

Between 2010 and 2023, the weighted rate rose from 49.8% to 52.9% in rural
counties and from 55.3% to 61.7% in nonrural counties, so the gap widened from
5.5 to 8.8 points. The series ends in 2023 because of NCES's publication lag.

```{r grad-rate-chart, echo = FALSE, eval = TRUE, out.width = "100%", fig.alt = "Line chart of cohort-weighted six-year completion rates from 2010 to 2023. Rural rises from 50 to 53 percent and nonrural from 55 to 62 percent, so both improve while the gap widens."}
knitr::include_graphics("figures/grad_rate.png")
```

## Awards versus students

The Completions survey includes two files: `C_A` counts **awards** and `C_C`
counts **students**. A student who earns two degrees at the same level counts
as one completer but two awards.

```{r completers}
completers |>
  group_by(variable) |>
  summarize(students = sum(value), .groups = "drop")
#>   variable                 students
#>   count_students_assoc       911084
#>   count_students_bach       1946263
#>   count_students_doctoral    215318
#>   count_students_masters     941849
```

Of the 4,137,499 degrees conferred, most of the gap between degrees and
students falls at the associate level, where degrees exceed students by roughly
10%. At every other level the difference is under 2%.

```{r completers-chart, echo = FALSE, eval = TRUE, out.width = "100%", fig.alt = "Grouped bar chart comparing degrees conferred with students completing at each award level. The gap is widest at associate level."}
knitr::include_graphics("figures/degrees_students.png")
```

## From degrees to occupations

Institution-level data retain NCES's detailed CIP program codes, which
`get_cip_soc_crosswalk()` maps to SOC occupation codes. Match the crosswalk
vintage to the completions year: `"2010"` for 2010–2019 and `"2020"` for 2020
onward.

```{r tech}
xw <- get_cip_soc_crosswalk("2020")   # CIP 2020 to SOC 2018

# SOC major group 15 is "Computer and Mathematical Occupations" -- 21 detailed
# occupations, from software developers to data scientists and statisticians.
#
# Collapse to a distinct CIP set FIRST. The crosswalk is many-to-many, so
# joining it to completions multiplies rows and inflates any sum afterwards.
cips <- xw |>
  filter(grepl("^15-", soc_code)) |>
  distinct(cip_code) |>
  pull(cip_code)

# Three years combined, to smooth year-to-year noise in small counties
tech <- get_degrees(geography = "institution", years = 2022:2024) |>
  filter(
    cipcode %in% cips,
    major_num == 1L,              # first majors only
    cipcode != "99.0000",         # drop NCES grand-total rows
    ed_level %in% c(3L, 5L, 7L, 17L, 18L, 19L)
  ) |>
  group_by(geoid) |>
  summarize(tech_degrees = sum(count_total_students), .groups = "drop")

rural |>
  left_join(tech, by = "geoid") |>
  mutate(tech_degrees = coalesce(tech_degrees, 0)) |>
  group_by(is_rural) |>
  summarize(degrees = sum(tech_degrees), .groups = "drop")
#>   is_rural degrees
#>   Nonrural  1111620
#>   Rural       89086
```

Across 2022–2024, rural counties produced 7.4% of degrees in programs that feed
computer and mathematical occupations. Of the 494 rural counties that produce
any, Merrimack County, NH, leads with 14,836.

```{r tech-chart, echo = FALSE, eval = TRUE, out.width = "100%", fig.alt = "Horizontal bar chart of the ten rural counties producing the most degrees in programs mapping to computer and mathematical occupations over 2022 to 2024, led by Merrimack County NH with 14,836."}
knitr::include_graphics("figures/tech_pipeline.png")
```


## Replicating this for your state

A county's `geoid` begins with its two-digit state FIPS code, which gives the
county set for a state; every getter then takes those geoids.

```{r state}
MY_STATE_FIPS <- "30"   # Montana

state_counties <- rural |>
  filter(substr(geoid, 1, 2) == MY_STATE_FIPS) |>
  pull(geoid)

get_degrees(geoids = state_counties, years = YR)
get_graduation_rates(geoids = state_counties, years = 2010:2023)
```
